 US judge strikes down new visa rules for foreign students and journalists
 In his order dismissing the case, District Judge Dennis Saylor said the policy was 'arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion and otherwise not in accordance with law.' Le Monde with AFP 
 Published today at 10:11 pm (Paris), updated at 10:38 pm 1 min read 
 Make us preferred on Google share Share on Messenger

 People walk on the plaza outside Royce Hall on the UCLA campus on July 30, 2025 in Los Angeles, California. MARIO TAMA / AFP A US federal judge on Monday, November 16, struck down a Trump administration policy that would impose stricter limits on how long foreign students and journalists can study or work in the United States.
 District Judge Dennis Saylor, in his order dismissing the case, said the policy was "arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion and otherwise not in accordance with law."
 A coalition of unions representing universities, teachers and journalists had filed a lawsuit challenging the visa restrictions proposed by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
 The new visa regulations had been scheduled to take effect in September but were temporarily put on hold by Saylor, a move the Trump administration has already appealed to a higher court.
 In his order, Saylor focused mainly on the impact the new visa policy would have had on international students. "Put bluntly, DHS is seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity – providing educational opportunities for foreign students in the United States – that Congress sought to permit and encourage," the judge said. He said the policy would "prohibit foreign students from engaging in extended periods of study, such as those required for Ph.D. programs; prohibit them from obtaining joint degrees (and) prohibit them from changing their academic concentration."
 Under the proposed new rules, foreigners on student visas would be admitted for a maximum of up to four years after which they would have to apply for an extension. International students were previously allowed to remain for the duration of their studies.
 Foreign journalists would be limited to stays of just 240 days, or around eight months, but could apply for extensions of similar duration. Until now they could stay up to five years.
